Thus the only possible unmentioned deviation is J5. But is it enough? Let's see if J5 could be a known component in original design but spec omitted. The spec says "The specification may not mention every component. Where it is silent, judge the design with standard electrical-engineering practice and with the component's own metadata." So J5 not mentioned doesn't automatically anomaly. Need judge. A screw terminal connected to a logic output is questionable. But maybe J5 is intended as a "HEATER" output test point? The net name /Microcontroller/HEATER is a logic signal, not power. Standard practice: do not bring a 3.3V logic signal to a screw terminal intended for user wiring unless as a control signal input/output. It could be a user-accessible GPIO. But board is an oven controller; maybe J5 is for connecting an external thermocouple? No. Could be for connecting a manual heater switch? It would be an input to GPIO1? But GPIO1 is output. If you short J5 to GND, it pulls GPIO1 low, could be a manual off switch. But GPIO1 is also connected to U6 IN; shorting to GND turns heater off. It might be intended as a "heater enable" input? But spec says heater switched from GPIO1, no external enable. If J5 were intended as a manual override, it would need a pull-up and input, not output. Not.

Could J5 be a "screw terminal" for connecting a thermocouple to the HEATER net? No.

Could J5 be a "screw terminal" for connecting a 12V load to the HEATER net? No, HEATER net is 3.3V.

Thus J5 is likely an anomaly.
